title: OpenDSU
lines: OpenDSU asks what must travel with data for it to remain controllable and verifiable.
The book explains a conceptual framework, rather than documenting one frozen software release.
Its central relationships connect protected content, authority, reconstructable structure, and verifiable history.
A cryptographic commitment can establish integrity without proving the truth of the content.
Readers gain distinctions for evaluating digital trust without asking one mechanism to guarantee everything.

title: What a copy leaves behind
lines: A copied file can retain its content while losing its history or policy.
A Data Sharing Unit instead gives related information an accountable logical boundary.
Protected bricks and a protected map support reconstruction of the object's contents.
Compact anchoring evidence records continuity without placing the confidential contents on a shared ledger.
The book explains why those relationships matter beyond any particular storage implementation.

title: Different rights, different proofs
lines: Reading, modification, and verification need not expose the same powers or information.
The book distinguishes capability, provenance, validation, and the context where authority is exercised.
Each mechanism answers a limited question about the digital object.
A valid history can still contain false claims or reflect an unacceptable process.
Those limits make the framework an argument about composed trust, rather than magical cryptography.

title: Read the relationships
lines: Begin with the verification gap before entering the technical vocabulary.
Follow the chapters on bounded objects, reconstruction, authority, and history as one connected design.
The evaluation chapter explains what each mechanism leaves unresolved.
OpenDSU is useful as a conceptual guide to controllable and verifiable information exchange.
Read it to judge which relationships your own digital objects need to preserve.
